entries.text:
Aldith doesn't stop kneading. "Edda Thorne's boy. She taught me to splint a rib when I was fifteen and she was already old. She said I had hands like a horse." She grunts. "Give me that."

She wipes one palm on her apron, takes the note, and reads it in a few seconds with her lips pursed. When she gets to the part about Wren, she reads it again.

"A twelve-year-old who sweeps a chapel nobody's asked her to sweep." She sniffs. "That's the right sort, or the sort that burns out by fifteen. Maud Marrow's vouching, is she? Maud's blankets are on my bed. I'll not insult her." She jabs a floury finger at you. "A month, then. Maud brings her when the roads are dry. She'll scrub, she'll carry, she'll hold the screaming ones down, and if she faints at the sight of bone I'll send her home. I'll not coddle her. And she keeps her mouth shut in my sickroom, whatever she sees."

Perrin gets a snort. "A dyer who fell off a rack and won't see a healer. Tell him to hobble down here by cart before the frost, and I'll break it and set it straight. It'll hurt worse than the fall. He'll curse me, and he'll walk right after." She wipes her hands at last. "And the boy with the ankle? Crushed, you say, not broken? Give me an hour. I'll see him this morning. Have Ansel bring him on the litter, and tell the little devil I've sweets in a jar for those who don't yell."

You have the time to say what you like. She watches you with sharp eyes, and her voice drops a notch. "You've the look of a man who hasn't slept well, healer. Anything else I ought to know about that bridge?"

It's about twenty to seven on Day 6. You have 800 XP and two 1st-level slots, and the town is waking up outside.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: she knew Edda's name. She agreed to see Tobin at once, wants a coin fee but is flexible for the poor, and said she'll read Brannoc's note about Wren. She grumbles but is curious about Perrin's crooked hip.

entries.text:
"Edda Thorne's." Mother Aldith wipes the flour from her hands onto her apron without taking her eyes off you. "Last I heard that woman was patching up half of a river town with one pair of hands and a tin of goose grease. She still alive?"

You tell her plainly that Edda died last winter, of old age, in her bed. Aldith is quiet for the length of a breath. "Good," she says gruffly. "Better than most get." She takes the note, reads it standing, mouth moving slightly, and snorts at the second line. "A girl who wants to learn. Aye. They all want to learn, till they've held a man's leg while I break it again."

She reads it a second time anyway.

"The boy first," she says. "A crushed ankle is a poor thing to leave a day, because the swelling sets the bones wrong. Bring him as soon as Ansel can spare a litter. I'll not have him walk. You've set him a drowsy-draught, I hope, and not a cure-all?" She sniffs when you say you've done nothing but keep him warm and hold the fear off. "Then you've done right."

On Perrin she is blunter. A month-old hip gone crooked is a hard thing, she says. She'd need him on her table, and she'd have to break it again and set it true, which is a bad fortnight for a man of his age and temper. "If he'll come, I'll do it. If he'll not, then no priest's prayer will straighten what's already knit." She jabs a floury finger at you. "Tell him I said that. Tell him Maud Marrow's blankets keep my feet warm, so I'll not be rough with him past what's needed."

As for Wren, she'll not promise. She wants to see the girl, her hands and her stomach, before saying aye or nay. "A month's trial is sound. Send her down with Maud when the weather holds. I'll feed her, I'll work her, and if she faints at the first break she can go home to her vats."

She looks at your mail and your mace and your amulet again, and then her expression sharpens. "You're the one who sealed the Drowned Stair last night. The whole town's talking of it." She jerks her chin at the pale bone over the door. "Don't think that buys you a discount. A silver for the ankle, a silver for my time. The boy's mother may not have it, so I'll take it from you if she hasn't, and mind you don't argue."

It's a little past half six in the morning. You have two healing prayers left, Channel Divinity ready, and 10 gp. Tobin's litter will take an hour or so to get here. You're 100 XP from level 3. The road back up the valley is long and the town has other hurts in it, if you want to look for them.

Aldith agrees to see Tobin today and wants Perrin Gale brought in person, but will not promise Wren a place on a paper: the girl must come herself, with Maud, and Aldith will judge her hands. entries.text:
She wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note between two floury fingers, and reads it standing, her lips moving. It takes her half a minute. Your pitch, spoken too fast and too hopefully, doesn't help. She folds the page small and tucks it into her sleeve.

"Edda's boy," she says. "Edda sent me two strays in her time, and one of them was a thief." She jerks her chin. "Tobin first. A crushed ankle in a nine-year-old can't wait on a sermon. Get the lad here on his litter and I'll look at him before the bread's out of the oven. Gods help him if the bones have knit wrong already."

Then she gives you the rest, flatly. A hip that's healed crooked in a man of Perrin's age is a hard business. She won't send for him or ride out for him, and he must come himself, on a cart, with someone to carry him home, or he can stay crooked and be damned. As for Wren, she won't promise a place to a girl she's never seen on the word of a stranger's note, however kind the stranger. "Send her, with Maud Marrow. I'll look at her hands. If she's quick and doesn't faint, she can stay a week. If she's useful at the end of it, we'll talk of more. And she'll sweep my floors like the rest." She sniffs. "Tell her that. Weak stomachs and soft hearts are two a penny. I want a steady one."

It isn't the yes you wanted, but it isn't a no either. She doesn't ask you for coin. She points at the flour with her chin. "Now, are you any use with dough? No? Then go and fetch me the boy."

It's about twenty to seven on Day 6. You have two 1st-level slots, Channel Divinity, and 800 XP. The hospice is a few streets away. Rudd, Imma and Tobin are waiting there, and the bridge was quiet in the night. Greywater and the rest of the valley road are still behind you.

Mother Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She grunts at "Edda Thorne's foster-son" and jerks her chin for the note, so you lay it on the table beside the bowl. She reads it with floury fingers, lips moving.

"Edda Thorne," she says. "Her splints were the neatest in three valleys, and she never once sent me a patient who wasn't worth my time. Which is more than I can say for most." She sniffs. "The boy first. Crushed, you say? Any bone out of line, or all pulp?"

You tell her what you saw. The swelling, the bruising, and the gray finger-marks that have faded now. She asks sharp questions about the colour of his toes and whether he could feel her prod, and you answer as well as you can. By the end she is nodding. She has wiped her hands and put on a leather apron before you finish. "I'll see him now. Carry him here if he can't walk. Ansel's good, but his hands are for the dying and mine are for the broken."

Then she reads the note again, slowly. "A dyer's girl who sweeps a chapel nobody asked her to sweep. Hm." She looks you in the eye. "Twelve's young. They cry at the first leg they have to saw. Some of them stay anyway." She taps the paper. "A month's trial, with Maud Marrow along, for I owe that woman a winter's worth of blankets and her word is gold. I'll take her if she comes. The water is black and still, and the reeds are dry and loud against the hull. You sit amidships with your shield on your arm, a flask of oil by your knee, the rope coiled, and the hooded lantern lit but dimmed. The village shrinks behind you to a smudge of smoke.

Boot-prints lead up from the boat through the cut stubble and then bend away around the mound's flank toward the west. Beside them runs a drag-mark, two parallel furrows in the mud, as of a man dragged by the heels, or a man too weak to walk.

The Wick-fires hang where they were, three low pale glows over the west side. They hold still. They don't come nearer. The reeds around them are bleached and grey. It's cold here, a damp, bone-deep cold, though the air is not moving.
